title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 9
paragraphs: Having so spoken, he stopped. After him Mardonius said: “Master, you surpass not only all the Persians who have come before you but also those who shall come after, for in your speech you have attained what is best and truest in other matters as well, and you will not allow the Ionians who dwell in Europe to make mockery of us with no just right to do so. It would be strange indeed if, after subduing and making our servants the Sacae, Indians, Ethiopians, Assyrians, and many other great nations who had done no wrong to the Persians but whom we conquered because we wanted to extend our rule, we should not take revenge on the Greeks who did wrong to us without provocation. What should we fear? What concentration of numbers? What resources in money? We know their way of fighting, and we know that their resources are feeble. Moreover, we have already subdued their children — I mean those who are settled in our land and are called Ionians, Aeolians, and Dorians. I myself tried the experiment before, when your father ordered me to march against them. I advanced as far as Macedonia, and came within a little of reaching Athens itself, and no one opposed me in battle. Yet the Greeks, from what I am told, do indeed wage wars, but very much without wise consideration, out of obstinacy and inexperience. When they declare war on one another, they find the fairest and smoothest piece of ground, come down to it, and fight — so that even the winners come off with heavy losses, and the losers I shall not even mention, for they are utterly destroyed. They ought, being men who speak the same language, to use heralds and messengers to take up their differences and settle them by any means rather than by battle; but if they absolutely must fight, they ought to find out each side the place in which they are hardest to overcome, and try their strength there. But the Greeks make no such good use of these methods: when I marched as far as Macedonia, they did not even come to the decision to fight. Who, then, is likely to set himself against you, O king, and offer war, when you are leading both all the multitudes of Asia and the whole of the fleet? I for my part am of the opinion that the power of the Greeks has not reached such a pitch of boldness. But if I should prove mistaken in my judgment, and if they, stirred up by thoughtless folly, should come to battle with us, they will learn that we are the best of all men in the arts of war. However that may be, let no means be left untried. Nothing comes of itself; everything comes to men through trial.”
